title: Living ashtpadi 16
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 17, salok: true in the beginning

segments.voice: Yesterday, known by the one He blesses, and your line: known by grace. Did a good thing arrive that you didn't earn? Today we close the sixteenth ashtpadi by living it, in the simplest place there is. Day five hundred one.
screen: `KNOWN BY THE ONE HE BLESSES — KNOWN BY GRACE.`

segments.voice: Picture an empty room. Not a cluttered one; a properly empty one, the way an apartment looks the day before you move in. Bare floor, bare walls, a window. What's in it? Nothing, you'd say. But that's not quite right. The room is full of space. You can't see the space, can't paint it, can't pick it up. And yet it's the only reason the room is any use. You'll put a bed in it, a table, a life, and every one of those things will sit inside that invisible, shapeless room-ness. Today: formless, yet everywhere.
screen: `AN EMPTY ROOM.` → `WHAT'S IN IT? NOTHING.` → `ACTUALLY, FULL OF SPACE.`

segments.voice: This week's salok said God has no form, no outline, no color, is beyond the three qualities, and is known by grace. Living that takes one more step, and Gurbani takes it constantly. The One is nirankaar, formless. Nir, without; aakaar, shape. It's one of the most common names for God in Sikh speech: Nirankaar. But Guru Arjan, elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib, pairs the two in one breath: formless, and Himself every form; without qualities, and with qualities, one. Nirgun and sargun. Both, at once. It sounds like a riddle. The empty room makes it less of one. Space has no shape. That's exactly why it can hold every shape. If space were square, round things wouldn't fit. Because it's nothing in particular, it can be around everything in particular. Sikhs often say this the other way round too: the One is sarab viaapak, pervading all. Not sitting at the top of the sky, but in and through every thing, the way space is in and through every room. That's why the formlessness isn't cold. A God with a shape would be over there, in a statue, a temple, a mountain. A formless God can't be over there, because there's no edge to stop at. Which means the One is also right here: in the kitchen, on the bus, in the hospital waiting room. And that changes what an empty room is. The quiet corner, the bare wall, the space between the furniture: for someone living the sixteenth ashtpadi, these aren't nothing. They're the clearest picture we have of what has no picture.
screen: `NIRANKAAR: WITHOUT SHAPE.` · `NIRGUN AND SARGUN, ONE.` · `SPACE HOLDS EVERY SHAPE.` · `NO EDGE, SO RIGHT HERE.` · then, large: `FORMLESS, EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in an empty room, or the emptiest corner you can find. Let your eyes rest on a blank stretch of wall or floor, or the air in the middle of the room. Don't look at things; look at the space between things. Notice that it's everywhere, around you, inside your cupped hands, between your breaths. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the name of that everywhere. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 16. Nirankaar, the Formless: no shape of its own, and so able to be in and through every shape, like space in an empty room.
Your line: formless, everywhere. Today, each time you walk through a doorway, notice the space of the next room before you notice the things in it. Day five hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs commonly call God Nirankaar, the Formless, and Gurbani describes the One as both nirgun and sargun, without and with qualities, pervading everything; gurdwaras keep no image of God.

myth: Gurbani says God is formless and also present in every form
nirgun and sargun, one: like space, shapeless and around every shape.
a formless God is far away, at the top of the sky
with no edge to stop at, the One is right here too.
Nirankaar is a rare name for God in Sikh speech
it's one of the most common.

fork.setup: how can the One have no form and yet be in every form?
options: it can't; one of those is wrong.
like space: no shape of its own, so it holds every shape.
fork.reveal: Gurbani pairs nirgun and sargun in one breath. space is nothing in particular, which is why it can be around everything.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nirankaar, the Formless, from nir (without) and aakaar (shape).

trapdoor: what you thought: formless means vague and far away.
what it means: with no shape of its own, the One is in and through every shape, here as much as anywhere.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's Gauri Bavan Akhri opens with nirankaar aakaar aap, nirgun sargun ek, holding both poles together.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 16 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 283–284)

notes: nirankaar aakaar aap, nirgun sargun ek: placed in Guru Arjan's Gauri Bavan Akhri at Ang 250; confirm.
